messages.subject: policy shortest-queue including server count?
parts:
The hospital simulation continues to grow (the trajectory plot is now
almost impossible to read!)
I've just added queueing for patients who can wait.

However, when selecting a policy to choose which ward to queue for I
noticed that the policy "shortest-queue" seems to include server count
as well as queue size when deciding what's shorter.

eg ward A - 30 patients being served (capacity 30), queue of 1
ward B - 20 patients being served (capacity 20), queue of 4

It appears as though the policy would choose ward B? Is there a
suitable policy that would choose A?

From simmer/inst/include/simmer/activity/resource_internal.h :

if (!selected || res->get_server_count() + res->get_queue_count() <
selected->get_server_count() + selected->get_queue_count())
selected = res;

Happy if I'm just misunderstanding this - I just have a lot of
patients queueing for one ward and trying to understand why!

tom

messages.subject: Re: policy shortest-queue including server count?
parts:
I've tested it with the enclosed code and it definitely seems to be
choosing something other than the shortest queue so I've filed an
issue for unexpected behaviour.


library(simmer)


env<-simmer()

patientA <- trajectory("fill ward A") %>%
seize("wardA") %>%
timeout(40) %>%
release("wardA")

patientB <- trajectory("fill ward B") %>%
seize("wardB") %>%
timeout(40) %>%
release("wardB")

patientC <- trajectory("which ward") %>%
select(c("wardA","wardB"),policy="shortest-queue-available") %>%
log_(function() {get_selected(env)}) %>%
seize_selected() %>%
timeout(40) %>%
release_selected


env %>%
add_resource("wardA",20) %>%
add_resource("wardB",30) %>%
add_generator("patientA", patientA, function() {c(rep(0.1,24),-1)}) %>%
add_generator("patientB", patientB, function() {c(rep(0.1,31),-1)}) %>%
add_generator("patientC",patientC, at(10)) %>%
run(80)


## With 24 patients in ward A, and 31 in B - queue size should be 4
for A and 1 for B
## expected behaviour: chooses ward B as that has the shortest queue
## actual behaviour: policy chooses ward A, until queue size for A
reaches 12 (ie 32 patients from the A generator)

> It seems I wrote that logic without considering resources with
> different capacities. Thanks for the report!

Thanks for looking into it - it was doing my head in trying to work
out why patients were "misbehaving"!

> > the trajectory plot is now almost impossible to read!
> You may want to break it down into several parts and then use join(). :)

I have join() all over the place unfortunately. Patients are tricky
and have lots of different behaviours to simulate in the model.

Two issues I'm having which might be ideas for future expansion:

1- rollback to a named point
eg within a trajectory have a rollback_point("foo") activity
later, we can rollback("foo") to rollback there.
As I'm tweaking things, I have to edit quite a few values across
different rollbacks (so far my highest is rollback(15)). This is
particularly an issue where I have a join() in there as I have to look
at that trajectory to see how many it adds to the rollback.


2-some more generic way of doing loops or making it possible to join()
or branch() to trajectories that haven't been defined yet
I appreciate this would probably be a massive undertaking as well as
slowing down everything, but at present only the trajectories defined
later can take advantage of join() and branch(), and everything
towards the top of the file is in a rollback() mess! Being able to
rollback to named points would probably solve a lot of this though.

tom

On Thu, 18 Jul 2019 at 12:09, Tom Lawton <t...@t-lawton.org> wrote:
>
> Two issues I'm having which might be ideas for future expansion:
>
> 1- rollback to a named point
> eg within a trajectory have a rollback_point("foo") activity
> later, we can rollback("foo") to rollback there.
> As I'm tweaking things, I have to edit quite a few values across
> different rollbacks (so far my highest is rollback(15)). This is
> particularly an issue where I have a join() in there as I have to look
> at that trajectory to see how many it adds to the rollback.

This is an excellent idea, and shouldn't be hard to implement. I have
a question for you though:

t1 <- trajectory() %>%
rollback_point("foo")
t2 <- trajectory() %>%
rollback("foo")
t3 <- join(t1, t2)

What would you expect here? Of course, I have an opinion already, but
I don't want to bias your expectations. ;-)

> 2-some more generic way of doing loops or making it possible to join()
> or branch() to trajectories that haven't been defined yet
> I appreciate this would probably be a massive undertaking as well as
> slowing down everything, but at present only the trajectories defined
> later can take advantage of join() and branch(), and everything
> towards the top of the file is in a rollback() mess! Being able to
> rollback to named points would probably solve a lot of this though.

About loops, I can't think of any more generic way of doing them
beyond a simple jump condition (as the rollback is; and the idea above
about labelling returning points will definitely improve its
usability), but suggestions are welcome.

On the other hand, I don't think that joining or branching inexistent
trajectories is a good idea. It requires NSE magic that complicates
things unnecessarily and breaks stuff. What you can already do is the
following:

t1 <- trajectory() %>%
seize("something") %>%
branch(function() 0, continue=TRUE) %>%
release("something")

option1 <- trajectory() %>%
timeout(1)
option2 <- trajectory() %>%
timeout(2)

t1[2] <- trajectory() %>%
branch(function() sample(2, 1), continue=c(TRUE, TRUE), option1, option2)

Note that it doesn't even need to be a branch (the first placeholder
in the definition of t1, I mean), because you can substitute any
activity with any other, as if trajectories were lists (they are in
some sense).

Iñaki

No, it shouldn't cross independent trajectories, because otherwise the behaviour is undefined if there are multiple definitions of the same label.

It should go backwards in the trajectory until the first matching label is found. The question is what happens if no proper label is found. The options are:

1) To continue at the top of the trajectory (with our without issuing a warning saying that no proper label was found).

2) To continue to the activity following the rollback (with our without issuing a warning).

3) To stop the simulation with an error 

Iñaki

Ok. And now, ignore t1 and t3. What would you expect if you insert an arrival into t2?

I guess that given my assertion they should be global in scope, the arrival should end up in t1. The only logical alternative I can see is to throw an error that there's no "foo" in this trajectory, which seems less useful.

No, it shouldn't cross independent trajectories, because otherwise the behaviour is undefined if there are multiple definitions of the same label.

It should go backwards in the trajectory until the first matching label is found. The question is what happens if no proper label is found. The options are:
If they were global you could throw an error when if a label is repeated. Having them local to a trajectory is equally valid but presumably you'll want to throw an error when:

t1 <- trajectory() %>%
 rollback_point("foo")

t2 <- trajectory() %>%

rollback_point("foo")

t3<- join(t1,t2) %>%
 rollback("foo")

Unless you define that it will always roll back to the first, or last, or most recent point (but even then I think a warning would be advisable)

 With rollbacks scoped to trajectories - in terms of what to do when the only matching rollback point is in a different trajectory or non-existent, I'd vote for throwing an error (option 3) as first choice, rolling to top of the trajectory with a warning (option 1) as second choice. Option 2 seems to fail the principle of least surprise, to me.

tom
